blocks: Change pitch scope: The keyboard and a sequence already modulate oscillator pitch at one volt per octave. Routing Key/Arp to Pitch can widen sequence steps to two or four semitones; negative modulation can shrink them to microtonal intervals.
Sum modulation signals: Combine the Standard and Cycling Envelope outputs at one destination to create a complex control signal for the filter or arpeggiator rate.
Mix the Cycling Envelope and LFO: Combining them at Filter Cutoff creates a composite modulation that can behave in surprising ways.
Modulate the Digital Oscillator: Let an unsynced LFO and Cycling Envelope control Wave, Timbre, and Shape at different speeds to create evolving timbral patterns.
Create regular automatic transpositions: Use the LFO's Random wave to modulate Pitch, or a slow square wave for more regular transpositions. The square-wave approach also works with a sequence.

Modulate modulation: Sequencer modulation tracks can change the strength of a Matrix connection. Hold an Assign button, select a Matrix point, then release the button to set that point as a destination. The LFO and Cycling Envelope can also modulate connection strength.
Modulate Cycling Envelope timing: Use the LFO to control its own rate, or use the Cycling Envelope to control its own rise time, fall time, or amount.

Create circular routings: Let the LFO control the Cycling Envelope's rise or fall time, then let the Cycling Envelope control its own level. The EMS Synthi became known for these distinctive, difficult-to-repeat routings.

The Digital Oscillator is the very heart of the MicroFreak. It's the digital circuit that generates the core sound of this instrument. The other parts of the MicroFreak - the Analog Filter, the Envelopes, and the LFO - exist only to shape/mangle/wobble the sound of the Digital Oscillator.

Oscillators come in two flavors; analog and digital. Digital oscillators have advantages over analog oscillators: they are capable of generating a much broader palette of waveforms and are more flexible and stable than their analog counterparts. Analog filters, on the other hand, have something special to them.
The MicroFreak offers you the best of both worlds: a digital oscillator and an analog filter.

The Oscillator in the MicroFreak is unique in that it can emulate many different synthesis models. In the history of electronic music, many gifted sound engineers developed unique ways of generating sounds. At Arturia, we are fans of Mutable Instruments. They permitted us to implement some of their open-source Oscillator designs in the MicroFreak, for which we are very grateful as they add a lot to the sonic potential of the MicroFreak.

The BASS, SAWX and HARM have been developed by Noise Engineering. The oscillators are special versions of the oscillators included in Noise Engineering's Virt Iter Oscillator Platform. The Virt Iter comes with these same three oscillator models but can be flashed with other models.

When you hear a sound, you hear air vibrating against the eardrum of your ear. As humans, we can hear frequencies in the range of 20 to 20,000 Hz. As you age your ability to hear high frequencies will gradually diminish. At 65 you'll probably hear only frequencies up to 6000 Hz. But that is enough to be able to enjoy timbral variations in music.
06.01 The oscillator as a sound generator

The ear can perceive sound around 50 Hz as bass (think huge organ pipes), but around 30 Hz it's difficult for the ear to hear a sound as a pitch; it's perceived as a low rumble. In electronic music, low-frequency sounds are often used as voltage or control signals to modulate another module. An LFO is an oscillator specifically designed to generate frequencies in this range. The LFO in the MicroFreak can generate signals in the range from 0.1Hz to 100Hz. Please refer to Microfreak/UG/08 LFO for details.

The parameter controls bring the Digital Oscillator to life in different ways.

Type selects an oscillator model, each with its own character. Type can also be modulated: changing models rapidly with the LFO creates abrupt changes in timbre. The Envelopes, keyboard pressure, Sequencer, and Arpeggiator can modulate Type too.
Changing Type shows that model and its current values on the display.

Each model has three sound-shaping parameters: Wave, Timbre, and Shape. Their effects depend on the model. Turning a knob shows its current function on the display; the oscillator overview uses those display names and puts the model's screen name in parentheses.
Wave, Timbre, and Shape can each be a modulation destination in the Matrix, so a sound can change as the modulation changes.

Wave, Timbre, and Shape knobs can track in Slow (the default) or Fast mode. Set the speed with Utility → Browsing → Osc Knob Speed, or on the Device Tab in Arturia's MIDI Control Center when the MicroFreak is connected.
Hold Shift while turning one of these knobs to use the opposite speed temporarily: Fast when set to Slow, or Slow when set to Fast.
Slow allows precise sound-design edits; Fast suits broader changes during a performance. In either mode, the knobs accelerate when turned more quickly.

The oscillator models from V.Analog through Noise were developed by Mutable Instruments and introduced in its Plaits module in 2018. Arturia included these open-source designs in the MicroFreak. For more detail about the waveforms, see the Plaits manual.

Description: Every sound consists of a series of harmonics. The first harmonic is the fundamental, which determines the pitch you hear. The second harmonic is twice as high in pitch, the third is three times as high, and so on. On a guitar, touching the exact middle of a string produces the second harmonic; dividing the string into three parts produces the third harmonic.
